Learning Objectives
Describe the basics of bone cell biology.
Compare types of bone (intramembranous, endochondral, cancellous, and cortical).
Assess the role that hormones, nutritional factors, and sunlight play in supporting bone mass.
Review the pathophysiology and determine diagnosis and treatment options for common
metabolic bone diseases, including osteoporosis, Paget disease of bone, rickets and
osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, osteogenesis imperfecta, fibrous dysplasia, and
osteopetrosis.

Bone is constantly reforming under the influence of:
Osteoclasts, which remove bone
Osteoblasts, which form bone
Osteocytes, which sense mechanical force on bone and coordinate the activity of osteoclasts
and osteoblasts to reshape bone to best resist mechanical force
Main Functions of Bone
It is the organ that provides structural integrity.
It is a storehouse for calcium and phosphate, which are critical components of many
biochemical processes.
It is the site of hematopoiesis.
Definition and Function of Osteoclasts
Multinucleated giant cell that derives from a common hematopoietic precursor (the monocyte)
(Figure 1)
Monocytes also give rise to macrophages and dendritic cells.
It is the only cell that can efficiently resorb bone.
Its size directly correlates with resorbing activity (larger osteoclasts with more nuclei are found
at very active resorption sites).
It is critically dependent on receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B ligand (RANKL) and colony
stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1) for its formation and function. CSF-1 also is known as macrophage
colony stimulating factor.
It is able to seal itself onto the resorbing surface and create a resorption space on bone with a
relatively low pH. This low pH facilitates the removal of bone mineral.
It uses lysosomal enzymes, particularly cathepsin K, which are active at low pH, to remove the
organic elements of bone (mostly type I collagen).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605

Figure 1 Illustration shows osteoclast development. RANK = receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ
B, RANKL = receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B ligand. (Reproduced with permission from
Tolar J, Teitelbaum SL, Orchard PJ: Osteopetrosis. N Engl J Med. 2004;351[27]:2839-2849.)

Definition and Function of Osteoclasts
RANKL and CSF-1 bind to their respective receptors on osteoclast precursor cells:
receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B and CSF-1R. A second soluble decoy receptor for
RANKL, osteoprotegerin, is produced in the bone microenvironment by osteoblasts and
inhibits resorption. Deletion of osteoprotegerin in animal models or as a cause of human
disease produces a phenotype of osteopenia or osteoporosis with enhanced osteoclastic
activity (Figure 2).
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
3/55

Figure 2 Illustration shows the attachment of an osteoclast to bone, which is facilitated
by podosomes containing filamentous actin and integrin alpha-v beta-3 (avß3). To
achieve acidification of the resorption lacunae and begin the process of bone
demineralization, carbonic anhydrase II (CAII) generates a proton and bicarbonate from
carbon dioxide and water. The proton is actively transported across the membrane of
the ruffled border through the action of the osteoclast-specific vacuolar-type H+–ATPase
proton pump. A chloride channel coupled to the proton pump facilitates balancing the
charge of ions across the membrane. Finally, excess bicarbonate is removed through the
basolateral membrane via passive exchange with chloride. The organic matrix of the
bone is removed via enzymatic activity, with cathepsin K playing a large role in this
process. (Reproduced with permission from Tolar J, Teitelbaum SL, Orchard PJ:
Osteopetrosis. N Engl J Med 2004;351[27]:2839-2849.)
Definition and Function of Osteoblasts
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
4/55

It is derived from a mesenchymal cell progenitor that also gives rise to marrow adipocytes and
marrow support cells.
The transcription factor Runx2 is critical for its differentiation from osteoprogenitor cells.
It is a mononuclear cell at the surface of bone, which secretes a complex matrix that is rich in
type I collagen.

Definition and Function of Osteoblasts
After it is secreted by osteoblasts, matrix mineralizes extracellularly under the influence
of the enzyme alkaline phosphatase, which also is produced by osteoblasts. Osteoblasts
increase production of RANKL and inhibit production of osteoprotegerin in response to
stimulators of resorption (parathyroid hormone [PTH], 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
(1,25[OH]2D), proinflammatory cytokines, and prostaglandins), which stimulates
osteoclast formation and function. Osteoblasts respond to local and systemic growth
factors (insulin-like growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, fibroblast growth factor
[FGF], etc.), which regulate their number and rate of bone formation. They are critically
dependent on the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway for their function. Wnts are a
family of locally secreted proteins (paracrine factors) that bind a receptor complex
containing lipoprotein receptor-related proteins 5 or 6 (LRP5/6) and frizzled protein.
Inhibitors of Wnt signaling that are produced in the bone microenvironment include
sclerostin and dickkopf-1. Diseases that inhibit Wnt signaling in osteoblasts decrease
bone mass (osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome, which are caused by a mutation in
LRP5). Conversely, diseases that enhance Wnt signaling in osteoblasts increase bone
mass (sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, which are caused by a loss of sclerostin).
Definition and Function of Osteocytes
They represent most bone cells.
They derive from osteoblasts that become encased in the calcified bone matrix.
They communicate with other osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts on the bone surface via
an interconnected complex of microscopic cell processes and bone channels called canaliculi.
They sense mechanical force and send signals to osteoclasts and osteoblasts on the endosteal
surface of bone to arrange the bone architecture to best resist the mechanical force (Wolff
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
5/55

Law).

Definition and Function of Osteocytes
Osteocytes produce factors that regulate osteoblasts (sclerostin, an inhibitor of Wnt
signaling) and osteoclasts (RANKL) on the surface of bone. They also produce the
phosphatonins, the most important of which is FGF-23. This regulates phosphate
handling and the activation of vitamin D in the kidney. In states of high bone turnover,
such as lactation, they can produce proteins that usually are associated with osteoclasts.
These allow osteocytes to produce a local resorptive lacuna around themselves.
Types of Bone
Intramembranous
Endochondral
Cortical
Trabecular or cancellous

Types of Bone
Intramembranous bone forms directly through the calcification of matrix, without a
cartilaginous intermediate. Examples are the bones of the skull, the mandible, and the
lateral one-third of the clavicle. Endochondral bone forms from a cartilaginous
precursor. Examples include most of the long bones. Cortical bone forms the dense
outer surface of long bones. It provides the greatest mechanical strength and has the
least surface area available for cellular remodeling. It typically represents approximately
80% of the bone mass. Trabecular or cancellous bone is the thin rod or plate-like bone
that is the most metabolically active because it has a greater surface-to-volume ratio
compared with cortical bone. Therefore, it has more surface on which osteoclasts can
resorb and osteoblasts can form bone. Areas of bone with a relatively high ratio of
trabecular to cortical bone (neck of the femur or vertebrae) are more prone to fracture
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
6/55

from diseases that involve bone loss, such as osteoporosis, because they have relatively
more surface area for bone cells to interact with (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustration shows that, during growth, chondrocytes mature and direct the
formation of new bone trabeculae in the process of endochondral bone formation and
osteoblasts form new bone via periosteal appositional growth. These processes
determine the length and width of bones. Bone is remodeled by osteoclasts (bone-
resorbing cells) coupled with osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) in basic multicellular units.
Bone remodeling is necessary to maintain calcium homeostasis and to renew bone to
repair microdamage and microcracks. The shape of bone is determined by the modeling
conducted by osteoblasts and osteoclasts. (Reproduced with permission from Canalis E,
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
7/55

Giustina A, Bilezikian JP: Mechanisms of anabolic therapies for osteoporosis. N Engl J Med
2007;357[9]:905-916.)
Hormones and Local Factors Affecting Bone
Role of PTH
PTH is produced by the chief cells of the parathyroid gland.
Its major function is to raise serum ionized calcium.

Role of PTH
The chief cells of the parathyroid gland sense serum ionized calcium levels via a specific
calcium-sensing receptor protein. Decreases in serum ionized calcium signal the chief
cells to produce and release PTH into the serum. Conversely, increases in serum-ionized
calcium have the reverse effect. The parathyroid gland maintains serum-ionized calcium
levels within a narrow band, which is critical for normal physiology. PTH functions to
stimulate bone resorption, decrease renal excretion of calcium, and stimulate renal
conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D) to its most active metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D
in the kidney.
Role of Vitamin D
Vitamin D is not a vitamin in the strictest sense of the definition because it is not an essential
nutrient.
The major function of vitamin D is to enhance gut absorption of calcium and phosphate.

Role of Vitamin D
Humans can produce vitamin D in the skin if exposed to adequate amounts of the sun’s
short wave-length ultraviolet radiation; however, migration of individuals from
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
8/55

equatorial regions (at which short wave-length ultraviolet light from the sun is abundant
year-round) to more temperate climates (which receive less year-round short wave-
length ultraviolet light) has made nutritional ingestion of vitamin D essential for many
individuals. In the northern half of the United States, it is difficult to produce vitamin D in
the skin in the winter because the sun remains relatively low in the horizon during the
day. This causes sunlight to pass through more of the atmosphere, compared with
summer, before it reaches the earth’s surface. The atmosphere filters ultraviolet
radiation; the more atmosphere that sunlight passes through, the less it is able to make
vitamin D in the skin. Vitamin D is a prohormone that is converted to a relatively weak
active metabolite in the liver (25[OH]D) and then to its most active form (1,25[OH]2D),
predominantly in the kidney but also, to a lesser degree, in many other organs.
Production of 25(OH)D is relatively unregulated and mostly dependent on vitamin D
stores. Conversely, production of 1,25(OH)2D is highly regulated. Vitamin D functions by
binding to specific vitamin D receptors, which in cells are predominantly found in the
cytoplasm or nucleus. After bound to its receptor, the complex initiates various signaling
mechanisms. In addition to regulating gut absorption of calcium and phosphate, the
active form of vitamin D also stimulates bone resorption. Two forms of supplemental
vitamin D are available: vitamin D3, which is the natural form, and vitamin D2, which is
derived from a plant sterol. Vitamin D3 has a longer half-life and is the preferred oral
supplement for patients.
Role of Calcitonin
Calcitonin is produced by the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland.
Its major function is to inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption.
Calcitonin inhibits bone resorption by binding to a specific receptor on osteoclasts and
inhibiting osteoclast formation.
Role of the Phosphatonins
These are a group of proteins that regulate phosphorous and vitamin D metabolism in the
kidney (Figure 4).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
9/55

The most well-studied phosphatonin, FGF-23, is made by osteocytes and acts on the kidney to
enhance phosphate excretion and inhibit the activation of vitamin D.

Figure 4 Illustration shows that vitamin D is initially generated in the skin via the nonenzymatic
conversion of provitamin D3 to previtamin D3. Dietary intake of vitamin D is usually relatively
limited because few foods, with the exception of certain types of fish, contain sizable amounts;
supplements are commonly used. Vitamin D is stored in adipose tissue or converted in the liver
by the enzyme 25-hydroxylase to 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (25[OH]D3), the form that circulates in
the highest concentration and reflects solar and dietary exposure. It is converted to the active
metabolite, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25[OH]2D), or calcitriol, in the kidney; however, other
tissues have 1.a-hydroxylase enzymatic activity. The synthesis of calcitriol is enhanced (+) by
increasing levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH), which rise in response to lower levels of serum
calcium. Reduced levels of serum phosphate also can increase (+) the production of calcitriol. Its
synthesis is suppressed (–) by the production of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23), which is
secreted by osteocytes in the bone matrix. Calcitriol inhibits the activity of 1.a-hydroxylase
(CYP27B1) and stimulates the activity of 24-hydroxylase (CYP24R1), an enzyme that promotes
production of 24,25(OH)2D3, a vitamin D product that is not biologically active. CYP = cytochrome
P. (Reproduced with permission from Rosen CJ: Clinical practice. Vitamin D insufficiency. N Engl J
Med 2011;364[3]:248-254.)
Effects of Genetics, Sex Steroids, and Age on the Skeleton
Genetic variabilities are one of the most powerful determinants of skeletal health.
Sex steroids are another important regulator of bone health.
Peak bone mass is achieved when individuals are in their twenties and typically declines after
age 50 years.

Effects of Genetics, Sex Steroids, and Age on the Skeleton
Substantial differences exist among ethnic groups with regard to the peak bone mass
that is achieved and the incidence of osteoporosis; however, current knowledge of the
gene polymorphisms that underly these differences is very limited. Women usually
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
12/55

achieve a lower peak bone mass than men. In addition, women go through menopause
and lose most of their sex steroids. Because of menopause, women have a more
accelerated rate of bone loss in the period after menopause and are more prone to
osteoporotic fragility fractures later in life. Conversely, men lose their sex steroids more
gradually during the geriatric period and have a lower incidence of osteoporosis. In
women, the loss of sex steroids with menopause accelerates the rate of bone loss for
approximately 10 to 15 years. After that, rates of bone loss in women and men are
similar. Bone quality, which is the ability of a bone to resist mechanical force without
fracturing, also declines with age in men and women.
Metabolic Bone Diseases
Osteoporosis
This is a disease of low bone mass and/or poor bone quality (Figures 5-12).
Affected individuals are at increased risk for a fragility fracture.
The lifetime risk of an osteoporotic fractures of the hip, spine, or wrist after age 50 years is
approximately 40% in women and 13% in men.1
Both genetics and sex steroid status are major determinants of the risk of osteoporosis in any
individual.
Secondary osteoporosis is defined as that caused by conditions other than aging or the loss of
sex steroids.
Bone density measurement via dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) remains the
preferred method for evaluating bone mass.
Medical therapies for osteoporosis include two broad classes of drugs: antiresorptive agents
and bone anabolic agents.
Antiresorptive agents
Diphosphonates
Raloxifene
Calcitonin
Anabolic agents
Teriparatide (an analog of human PTH consisting of amino acids 1 to 34 from the N
terminus)
Abaloparatide (an analog of PTH-related peptide with similar activity to teriparatide)
9/3/26, 4:43 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
13/55

Romosozumab (a neutralizing antibody to sclerostin, which enhances Wnt signaling and
has anabolic and anti-resorptive activity)

(rectangle), Ward area (square), and trochanter. Each region of interest is defined and analyzed


Osteoporosis
A fragility fracture is defined as a fracture that is produced by a force that would not be
expected to cause a fracture in a normal individual. An example is a fracture sustained
during a fall from a standing height. Frequent sites of osteoporotic fragility fractures are
the vertebrae and the neck of the femur. These have a relatively high ratio of trabecular
to cortical bone, which means that these bones have relatively more sites for osteoclasts
to interact with bone mineral and produce bone loss. Osteoporosis occurs if rates of
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
22/55

bone resorption exceed rates of bone formation, causing local or systemic bone loss, or
if bone quality, which is defined as the inherent ability of bone to resist fracturing during
exposure to mechanical force, is below a threshold, causing the risk of fracture to be
considerable.
Examples of secondary osteoporosis include glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and
osteoporosis associated with inflammatory diseases, malignancy, type I (insulin-
dependent) diabetes mellitus, osteogenesis imperfecta in adults, unmanaged long-
standing hyperthyroidism, chronic malnutrition, malabsorption, or chronic liver disease.
Medications, such as heparin, proton pump inhibitors, aromatase inhibitors, certain
antidiabetic drugs, and immunosuppressives, also are associated with an increased
incidence of osteoporosis. Initial diagnostic workup includes a careful history of the
patient and family members; evaluation of serum vitamin D levels, sex steroid levels,
thyroid hormone levels, and calcium levels; a complete blood count, and serum protein
electrophoresis. The latter is performed to identify any individuals with multiple
myeloma.
In addition to bone mineral content, DEXA also measures soft-tissue composition.
Therefore, changes in soft tissue that occur with changes in weight may alter DEXA
measurements independent of changes in bone mineral content. The World Health
Organization has defined osteoporosis according to DEXA criteria alone as a bone
mineral density T-score that is more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean. The
T-score is a comparison of an individual's bone density with that of a healthy young adult
of the same sex. The Z-score is a comparison of an individual's bone density with that of
an average person of identical age and sex. T-score values between –1 and –2.5 are
defined as osteopenic; however, DEXA cannot measure bone quality, which is the
inherent ability of bone to resist fracturing. Almost 50% of postmenopausal women
older than 50 years who sustain an osteoporotic fracture do not have osteoporosis as
defined by bone mineral density criteria alone. To better assess the risk of fracture in an
individual, the World Health Organization created a computer algorithm called the
Fracture Risk Assessment Tool. This tool considers multiple criteria in evaluating the risk
for an osteoporotic fracture. The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool relies on a DEXA score at
the femoral neck and also considers the following additional risk factors: (1) body mass
index, (2) history of a previous fracture in the patient or a parent, (3) history of smoking,
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
23/55

(4) history of glucocorticoid use, (5) history of rheumatoid arthritis, (6) history of
secondary osteoporosis of any cause, and (7) history of alcohol consumption of three or
more units per day. General measures for treating patients with osteoporosis include
adequate intake of calcium, preferably via food; adequate levels of vitamin D, measured
as serum 25(OH)D3; and adequate weight-bearing exercise.
Examples of antiresorptive therapies, which inhibit osteoclastic activity, include the
diphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, and zoledronic acid); raloxifene,
a selective estrogen receptor modulator; and denosumab, a neutralizing antibody to
RANKL. Calcitonin also is available; however, its efficacy generally is much less than that
of other antiresorptive agents. For many years, estrogen replacement was prescribed to
treat women with osteoporosis; however, its use was discontinued after it was found to
be associated with an increased incidence of breast cancer and cardiovascular diseases.
The long-term use of potent antiresorptive agents, such as diphosphonates or
denosumab, has been associated with the development of rare but substantial
complications, including osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical subtrochanteric femoral
fractures.
Examples of bone anabolic agents include teriparatide, an analog of human PTH
containing the first 34 amino acids; abaloparatide, an analog of PTH-related protein; and
romosozumab, an antibody to sclerostin, which is a negative regulator of Wnt signaling.
Teriparatide and abaloparatide bind the PTH receptor 1 on osteoblasts. If administered
as a single daily injection, the effect of intermittent stimulation of PTH receptor 1 on
bone formation is greater than the effect on bone resorption, and a net gain of bone
occurs. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling by binding to LRP 5/6, preventing the binding by
Wnt proteins to this receptor. Romosozumab is an antibody that binds to sclerostin,
preventing sclerostin from interfering with Wnt signaling. This, enhances osteoblast
function. Wnt signaling also affects osteoclast function, and evidence suggests that
romosozumab inhibits bone resorption in addition to its anabolic effects on bone
formation.
Paget Disease of Bone
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Metabolic Bone Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000605
24/55

The disease is believed to originate via the formation of uncontrolled large osteoclasts in one
or multiple bones (Figures 13-16).
These initial lytic lesions typically progress to become sclerotic with lytic components, forming
disorganized bone.
Lesions rarely progress from the bone in which they were originally detected to other bones of
the skeleton.
The disease usually is not clinically apparent until age 50 to 60 years.
The diagnosis of Paget disease may be made via an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase
concentration or after a routine radiograph.
It usually is advisable to determine the extent of skeletal involvement by performing a whole-
body radionucleotide bone scan as part of the initial workup.
The disease has proven very amenable to treatment with antiresorptive agents, and
intravenous or oral diphosphonates generally are considered the first line of therapy.

The most common symptom of a Pagetic lesion is pain; however, it also may be
associated with fracture, skeletal deformities, deafness, and other neuropathies

Management typically is associated with complete control of pain; however, persistence
of bony deformities and deafness, if present, is typical. Because of the high blood flow
into the lesions, high output cardiac failure occasionally is associated with Paget disease
of bone. The pathophysiology of Paget disease of bone is associated with a strong
genetic component, which is associated with mutations in the SQSTM1 gene. Controversy
exists about an initiating viral event in the pathogenesis of Paget disease of bone
because of the finding by some investigators that involved cells expressing proteins,
which are found in certain viruses, particularly measles.
Rickets and Osteomalacia
Rickets and osteomalacia are diseases of inadequate mineralization of bone matrix. They most
often result from a deficiency of vitamin D (Figure 17).
In adults, the disorder is termed osteomalacia and involves only bone.
In children, the disease is termed rickets, and abnormalities also are found in the growth plate
and in the mineralization of cartilage, leading to characteristic deformities.
Individuals with darker pigmented skin are more prone to these diseases because skin
pigment filters short ultraviolet light, reducing the efficiency of skin to make vitamin D.
The diagnosis of vitamin D deficiency rickets or osteomalacia typically is made via a low serum
25(OH)D level.
Therapy is with supplemental vitamin D (preferably vitamin D3).
Standard laboratory tests measure bound vitamin D, not free vitamin D.

Rickets and Osteomalacia
Rickets and osteomalacia also can be caused by metabolic defects in the vitamin D
hormone system. These include inadequate activation of vitamin D in the liver and
kidney because of a gene defect or an acquired disease of these organs. In addition,
abnormalities of the vitamin D receptor may be a cause. Mineralization may be impaired
if the supply or transport of mineral, particularly phosphate, is impaired in renal,
intestinal, or bone cell disorders. X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets is most frequently
caused by a mutation in the PHEX gene, which leads to increased levels of the
phosphatonin FGF-23. This results in low levels of serum phosphate because of
increased phosphate excretion by the kidney and inadequate activation of 25(OH)D to
1,25(OH)2D. Rickets is characterized by deformities of the long bones, growth plates, and
ribs. Classic findings are widened growth plates, irregular metaphyses, and loss of
definition of the zone of provisional calcification. In adults, typical radiographic signs are
pseudofractures and subperiosteal resorption. In children and adults, serum calcium
levels tend to be low, and serum PTH levels tend to be elevated.
The development of osteomalacia as a result of a malignancy, which often is an occult
lesion, is termed oncogenic osteomalacia. It frequently results from the production of
the phosphatonin FGF-23 by the tumors. This impairs mineralization by increasing renal
phosphate excretion, lowering serum phosphate, and by interfering with the activation
of vitamin D.
Hypophosphatasia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that presents with a rachitic
phenotype. It is characterized by mutations in the gene for alkaline phosphatase, which

Hyperparathyroidism
The disease is caused by the excessive production of PTH.
It is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in the general ambulatory population.
The incidence increases with age and is most common in individuals older than 50 years.
Most often, this condition results from a single adenoma or, more rarely, multiple adenomas
in one or more of the four parathyroid glands in the neck.
Overproduction of PTH increases serum total and ionized calcium and lowers serum
phosphorus levels.
The diagnosis is made via elevated levels of serum total or ionized calcium and inappropriately
elevated or mid- to high-normal range levels of intact serum PTH. Urine excretion of calcium
also is typically elevated.
Bone in patients with hyperparathyroidism typically demonstrates high turnover with
increased rates of resorption and formation, resulting in a higher proportion of cancellous
bone relative to cortical bone. This may weaken bone quality, leading to an increased risk of
bone fracture.
The preferred therapy for almost all causes of true hyperparathyroidism is surgical removal of
the lesions in the parathyroid glands.
Calcimimetics (cinacalcet and etelcalcetide) are small molecule drugs that activate the calcium-
sensing receptor, independent of calcium, in parathyroid chief cells to reduce production of
PTH.

Hyperparathyroidism
In patients with end-stage renal disease, phosphate levels may be elevated. This may
cause soft-tissue calcifications, which lower serum ionized calcium levels. In addition,
activation of vitamin D is impaired, reducing the efficiency of gut absorption of calcium.
The result often is the development of secondary hyperparathyroidism to raise serum
calcium levels. Measurement of serum PTH in patients with renal failure is complicated
by the accumulation of inactive PTH fragments that normally are excreted by the kidney.

Familial benign hypercalcemia (familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia) is an autosomal
dominant condition that most often is caused by a heterozygous loss of function
mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor. This condition is characterized by mild
hypercalcemia, normal to mildly elevated serum PTH levels, and extremely low levels of
calcium in the urine. Currently, genetic analysis of the calcium receptor is available to aid
in the diagnosis. Identification of patients with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is
important because surgical treatment is not indicated and should be avoided.
Calcimimetics are effective therapies for hyperparathyroidism because adenomatous
parathyroid cells reset the calcium sensing mechanism so that higher than normal levels
of serum ionized calcium are required to inhibit PTH production. Calcimimetics are
indicated in: patients with end-stage renal disease, patients who have parathyroid
malignancies that are responsive to the level of ionized calcium, and patients with
hyperparathyroidism who are not surgical candidates.
Osteogenesis Imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a congenital disorder in which increased bone fragility leads to
fractures and deformity (Resource 1). Severity is highly variable. Mild cases may only be
detected in late adulthood, whereas severe cases can cause fractures in infants during
childbirth or in children (Figures 18-25).
Most patients with osteogenesis imperfecta have defects in one of the two genes for type I
collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2).
Currently, therapy is limited to antiresorptive agents; however, the efficacy of diphosphonate
therapy to prevent fractures in this disease is controversial.

Fibrous Dysplasia
Fibrous dysplasia most often presents as an expanding lesion within the bone, containing
fibroblastic and osteoblastic cells (Figure 26).
The disorder may be monostotic, without associated abnormalities, or polyostotic, which may
be part of McCune-Albright syndrome.
It is because of an activating mutation of the Gs alpha regulatory protein that stimulates the
enzyme adenyl cyclase, causing constitutive action of cyclic adenosine monophosphate.
Therapy is variable, depending on whether the lesions are stable or expanding, and may
involve surgical management or a course of antiresorptive therapy.

Osteopetrosis
Mutations in the TCIRG1, CLCN7 and OSTM1 genes, which influence acid generation, are
found in many patients with autosomal recessive osteopetrosis who have dysfunctional

osteoclasts. Patients with dysfunctional osteoclasts and intermediate autosomal
recessive osteopetrosis or benign autosomal dominant osteopetrosis also may have
mutations in CLCN7. Patients with intermediate autosomal recessive osteopetrosis may
have mutations in carbonic anhydrase II, which catalyzes acid generation, or PLEKHM1,
which is involved in vesicular trafficking. Mutations in the genes for receptor activator of
nuclear factor-κ B (TNFRSF11A) and RANKL (TNFSF11) have been described in patients
with autosomal recessive osteopetrosis who lack osteoclasts. Another cause of
osteopetrosis with dysfunctional osteoclasts is inactivating mutations in the cathepsin K
gene. This produces the disease pyknodysostosis. Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis
type I is the result of mutations in the LRP5 gene. These prevent sclerostin from
inhibiting Wnt signaling pathways. In patients with osteopetrosis because of
dysfunctional osteoclasts or receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B deficiency,
hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from an unaffected individual may be helpful.
